🪵 PART A:
Chronic Pancreatitis

1. Definition &
Etiology

Definition: Irreversible destruction and progressive
fibroinflammatory transformation of the pancreatic
parenchyma, leading to permanent loss of both
exocrine and endocrine functions
Etiology:

Chronic Alcohol Abuse: Most common cause overall
(up to 90%). Induces protein plugs that block ductules,
reducing vascularity and triggering chronic ischemia

Biliary Obstruction: Recurrent gallstones impacted
at the lower end of the CBD

Congenital/Anatomical Anomalies:
e.g., Pancreas Divisum (failure of dorsal
and ventral buds to fuse)

Other Causes: Hereditary pancreatitis,
hypercalcemia, direct pancreatic trauma,
or localized malignancies

2. Clinical
Presentation

The Signature Pain: Severe epigastric pain
radiating straight to the back. Continuous or intermittent.
Classically exacerbated by meals (intraductal pressure
elevation behind fibrotic duct strictures)

Malabsorption & Steatorrhea: Loss of exocrine cells
(lipase deficiency). Stools become bulky, greasy, soft,
highly foul-smelling, and difficult to flush

Type-3 Diabetes Mellitus: Develops in 1/3 of patients
due to chronic inflammatory destruction of beta-islet cells.
Highly brittle, notoriously unstable,
usually requires insulin

Obstructive Jaundice (3% of cases): Occurs if severe
fibrosis of the pancreatic head compresses the adjacent CBD

3. Diagnostic
Workup

Fecal Elastase Levels: The most sensitive test to
confirm and quantify pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
High fat content in stools documents steatorrhea

Plain Abdominal X-ray: May demonstrate pathognomonic
pancreatic calcifications along the ductal system

ERCP & MRCP: Reveal the classic "chain of lakes"
appearance — alternating strictures and segmentally
dilated areas along the main pancreatic duct

Glucose Tolerance Test (GTT): Indicated to screen
for underlying endocrine insufficiency (Type-3 DM)

4. Management
Strategies
Conservative Management:
Strict and immediate avoidance of alcohol

Chronic pain control using non-opioid analgesics
(Aspirin, Paracetamol)

Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT):
Oral lipase (10,000–12,000 units per meal).
Must be given with a PPI or H2-blocker to prevent
gastric HCl from denaturing the enzyme extract

Daily supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins
(A, D, E, and K)
Surgical Intervention:

Absolute Indication: Severe, persistent, and
refractory abdominal pain that fails
conservative medical therapy

Lateral Pancreaticojejunostomy (Puestow Procedure):
Standard drainage operation for diffuse ductal involvement.
Main duct opened longitudinally head to tail
and anastomosed to a loop of jejunum

Distal Pancreatectomy: Indicated for localized
chronic inflammatory lesions strictly confined
to the tail of the pancreas

Whipple Procedure: Reserved for localized disease
or a fibrotic mass isolated to the head of the pancreas

🚗 PART B:
Pancreatic Trauma

1. Pathophysiology
& Mechanisms

Location Danger: Deeply nestled in the retroperitoneum.
Provides physical protection but injuries are notoriously
missed on initial physical exams and CT scans,
leading to high morbidity and delayed diagnosis

Anatomical Danger: Rarely isolated. Highly associated
with injuries to adjacent retroperitoneal organs and
major vessels (stomach, duodenum, lower CBD,
aorta, SMA/SMV)
Mechanisms of Injury:

Blunt Trauma (more than 70%): Direct force to
epigastrium (steering wheel, bicycle handlebar,
sports cart). Compresses pancreas against vertebral
column causing laceration/transection at the neck

Penetrating Trauma (less than 30%): Direct laceration
from gunshot wounds (GSWs) or stab wounds

2. Diagnostic
Approach

Clinical Presentation: Isolated pancreatic trauma
(10%) may be initially asymptomatic. Other 90% present
with associated injuries, hemorrhagic shock, or peritonitis.
Delayed adynamic ileus signals retroperitoneal hemorrhage

Serum Amylase: Neither sensitive nor specific for
acute trauma. Amylase can rise in any abdominal
catastrophe (e.g., perforated bowel)

CT Scan with Contrast: Primary staging modality.
Initial CT can miss early ductal disruption.
Repeat CT is mandatory if patient fails to improve

Ductal Integrity Evaluation: Status of the main
pancreatic duct is the single most critical factor
in management. ERCP is more sensitive and specific
than MRCP for identifying subtle ductal lacerations

3. Lucas
Classification

Class I: Simple superficial contusion or peripheral
parenchymal laceration. Intact main pancreatic duct

Class II: Deep laceration, perforation, or transection
of the pancreatic neck, body, or tail.
With or without duct injury

Class III: Severe crush injury, perforation, or
transection of the pancreatic head.
With or without ductal injury

Class IV: Combined complex pancreaticoduodenal
injuries (severe head injury + duodenal injury
+ ductal disruption)

4. Management
Algorithm

Minor Injuries (Intact Duct / Class I):
Conservative (non-operative) with NPO,
IV fluid resuscitation, and closed suction
drainage if necessary

Major Injuries (Ductal Disruption / Class II, III, IV):
Mandates surgical exploration to prevent uncontrolled
pancreatic ascites or severe retroperitoneal necrosis
Surgical Techniques:

Distal Pancreatectomy (Body/Tail injuries):
If duct injury is distal to the superior mesenteric
vessels. Spleen may also be resected (splenectomy)
if splenic vessels are torn

Surgical Drainage (Head injuries / Class III):
Cautious debridement and placement of wide,
closed-suction retroperitoneal drains

Whipple Procedure (Pancreaticoduodenal / Class IV):
Last resort for devitalizing injuries to pancreatic
head and duodenum. Emergency Whipple carries
extremely high mortality rate (20–40%)
